Chapter 41 – Lamps in the Fog

Fog rolled in from the harbor before dawn, swallowing the cranes one by one until only the nearest mooring posts remained, black and dripping, like the stumps of an old forest.

Wren had been awake for an hour already. She sat on the sea wall with her boots dangling over the water and listened to the bells of the fishing boats feeling their way home through the grey.

“You’ll catch your death,” said Oskar, lowering himself beside her with a grunt. He handed her a tin cup of tea so strong it was nearly black. “Or worse, you’ll catch a cold and complain about it for a week.”

“I never complain.”

“You complained about the tea yesterday.”

“The tea yesterday was terrible.” She drank anyway, letting the heat sink into her fingers. Somewhere out in the fog a horn sounded twice, low and mournful, and the gulls on the warehouse roofs answered it with a ragged chorus.

They watched the first lamps come on along the quay. The lamplighter moved from post to post with his long hooked pole, and each new light opened a small golden room in the mist, warm and private, before the fog closed its walls around it again.

“The ledger,” Oskar said eventually. “Did you find it?”

Wren reached into her coat and set the little book between them on the stone. Its cover was swollen with damp and one corner had been chewed by something with very small teeth, but the pages inside were dry and the columns of numbers were still sharp and clear.

Oskar did not touch it. He looked at it for a long time, the way a man might look at a sleeping dog he was not sure was friendly.

“Every ship that came in last spring,” Wren said quietly. “Every crate, every name. And every bribe, written down in the harbormaster’s own hand, as neat as a schoolboy’s homework.”

“Then he’s a bigger fool than I thought.”

“Or he wanted someone to find it.”

The horn sounded again, closer now. A shape was forming in the fog beyond the end of the pier, tall and slow, its masts like the bare branches of a winter tree. Neither of them moved as it drifted toward the quay, and neither of them said what they were both thinking: that the ship had no lamps lit at all.
